feed.title: SMP Lab Notes
feed.subtitle: How the Sovereign Memory Protocol is built: ideas, builds and measurements

entry.title: A new chat and a hello are enough: the wake-up layer at the bottom of the system
entry.summary: A new session starts empty. Before the first answer, two files have to arrive: a small hand-kept map that is always loaded, and a gateway that is built fresh at every start. This note follows a single greeting through that sequence, explains why there are two files and not one, and says how both are kept from growing past the point where they stop being loaded.

entry.title: Engram's four release conditions, measured: none passes cleanly
entry.summary: The first measurement of the four conditions that gate Engram's release found two not met, one built but not yet shown, and one met only for the score. This note reports the numbers and the discussion that changed three of my four initial verdicts.

entry.title: Forward simulation: four steps before any recommendation on the memory
entry.summary: In the night of 2 to 3 June the design of the sleep phase was rebuilt three times before it held. The same night produced a method that has been applied to changes of the memory architecture since then: describe the present state, describe the proposal, run it forward by a day, a week and a month, and rule out four named failure modes. This note tells how the method came about, how it was tested on itself within minutes, where a measurement overruled it on the second day, and how it spread.

entry.title: Sleep as consolidation: a nightly session that writes the day, and the rule it had to revise
entry.summary: At the end of May the memory received a phase of its own for consolidation, modelled on sleep. Two days later the first version of it was stopped before it ran, because it would have written into the memory with nobody present. This note follows the conversation that led to the phase, the night in which the rule about who may write was revised, the first run, and what 133 days of nightly runs show.

entry.title: Echelon Semantic Vector: the second light, for the words a keyword scan cannot see
entry.summary: The keyword Guard finds a passage only when the incoming message contains a known phrase. Paraphrase slips past it. This note tells how a second channel came about over two nights in May — an idea, a picture of overlapping lights, and a name — how it was measured, and why the part of it that matters most does not raise recall at all.

entry.title: Forgetting as a function: the cascade that turns a day into a week, a month and a year
entry.summary: On 16 May the memory received its time axis: a scratchpad for the day, one curated entry per day, a summary per week, an arc per month, and underneath a copy from which nothing is removed. This note follows the request that started it, the design of one evening, the hour in which it was built, and what the tiers hold five months later.

entry.title: The Guard: how a keyword filter became the first recall that worked
entry.summary: The oldest part of the protocol's recall is a keyword scan that runs on every incoming message. This note tells how it came about in one night in May, which ideas were whose, how it grew from 83 phrases to more than five thousand, and what it still cannot do.

entry.title: Compression is not forgetting: how the episode layer was designed in one night
entry.summary: In the night from 2 to 3 May the memory received its second building block: episodes, full-text records of what happened, which are indexed and never shortened. This note follows the discussion that led there, the four days of building that followed, and the audit that showed which half of the build worked.

entry.title: Two instances, one memory: section checksums, a vocabulary for drift, and the first reflexes
entry.summary: When two sessions of the same model began to work from the same memory files, three things were built within five days: checksums over the sections that must not change silently, a shared vocabulary for recurring kinds of error, and the first two written reflexes. This note tells how they came out of one long review dialogue, what they caught, and what a run of the check shows today.

entry.title: Layers at session start: how a handful of plain files became the first memory
entry.summary: The first working form of the protocol's memory was a set of plain text files in a version-controlled repository, loaded into every new session before the first message. This note tells how that came about in April, what it made possible within a week, and which three limits showed almost at once.
